- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts rise steadily, cap the upward slope to avoid overshoot after recent spikes.  
- If supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model should not overcorrect upward — expect mean reversion toward lower range.  
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >75), model should reduce forecast momentum for next 5–7 days to avoid lagged overreaction.  
- When bullish sentiment is high but supply net is negative, model should not assume sustained high prices — expect downward correction within 10–15 days.  
- If model forecasts are flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows strong volatility, adjust for sentiment-driven momentum shifts — especially after auction events.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from model in first 5 days, reset forecast anchor to recent 7-day average to reduce lag bias.  
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and supply net is negative, model should not overestimate bullishness — expect price to stabilize or dip.  
- If recent auction supply events are frequent (e.g., 3+ per 30d), model should reduce forecast slope — supply events suppress price momentum.  
- For 30d forecasts, if true outcome shows early dip (first 5 days) followed by recovery, model should not overestimate recovery — expect plateau or slight decline.  
- When bullish sentiment is high but true outcome shows early correction, model should not assume continuation — expect mean reversion within 7–10 days.
